title: ANIME WORKOUTS - Would Baki's training really make you gain 20lbs of muscle in t
summary: NH analyses Baki's mountain training arc in Grappler Baki, from his rejection of conventional gym training to rock-carrying hill sprints, push-ups, rope climbing and a massive eating regime. He judges what is plausible (calorie surplus, resistance, endorphin-driven work capacity) and what is impossible (20 lb of muscle in three months naturally) and warns about the injury risks of training through pain.
claims: Incline curls are not the best biceps exercise and are useless for a grappler; resting three minutes after one set of curls is excessive
Personal development is a lonely endeavour: if you need people cheering you on or friends to motivate you to train, you won't get very far
You cannot build muscle out of thin air; a skinny person who wants to gain needs a lot of calories, especially if young and very active
If you eat more than your caloric needs require you simply end up fat; intake must match expenditure
Muscle mass is metabolically expensive, so a very muscular, very active athlete can justify an enormous calorie intake
Gaining 20 lb of muscle in three months is absolutely impossible for anyone, especially a natural
Lots of muscle distorts the perception of body fat on a frame; visible arm and leg separation suggests around 10-12% body fat
The key to putting on mass is resistance: movements that are trivial unweighted damage the fibres when load is added
To build the legs you need knee flexion and hip hinging; lunges on an incline cover quads, hamstrings and glutes while staying athletic
Weighted uphill sprints on rocky terrain are very dangerous alone; dirt and leaves soften impacts on the knee ligaments, rocks don't and are slippery
Endorphins are real: intense exercise can trigger a release that blunts pain, the runner's high, and lifters experience it too
Pain signals exist to protect you; deliberately triggering endorphins to push past limits is not something amateurs should try
Striking trees to condition shins and knuckles risks breaking your hand; endorphins mask pain but don't protect from bone damage
Training all day with no breaks limits recovery windows to nights and invites muscle tears, tendon damage and tendinitis
A short, stocky build may reduce damage through better leverages and sturdier bones
Push-ups develop the entire chest, triceps and to an extent the shoulders
Rope climbing trains biceps and forearms; depending on grip and wrist/elbow flexion it becomes more limb-dominant, with lats and upper back always involved
Jumping off a cliff to boost reaction time is fiction; don't try it
Baki's 200 kg of food in three months implies roughly 8,000-10,000 kcal and over 2.2 kg of food per day, which would make most people obese
exercises: not the best biceps builder; useless for a fighter
knee flexion plus hip hinge for quads, hams and glutes while staying athletic
huge quad stress but dangerous alone
grip and wrist/elbow flexion change limb involvement; L-sit adds abs
